## Overview

`fineMappingPipeline()` is a single pipeline that can accept any of the
following inputs:

| Input class | What it represents | Methods supported |
|---|---|---|
| `QtlDataset` | Single-study individual-level data | susie, susieInf, susieAsh, mvsusie, fsusie |
| `MultiStudyQtlDataset` | Multiple `QtlDataset` objects (optionally with an embedded `QtlSumStats`) | susie, susieInf, susieAsh, mvsusie, fsusie (individual-level only), ser (via an embedded `QtlSumStats`) |
| `QtlSumStats` | QTL summary statistics annotated by `(study, context, trait)` | susie, susieInf, susieAsh, mvsusie, ser |
| `GwasSumStats` | GWAS summary statistics annotated by `study` | susie, susieInf, susieAsh, ser |

Method arguments are the same across input classes; `fineMappingPipeline()`
routes `methods = "susie"` to `susieR::susie` for individual-level data
and to `susieR::susie_rss` for summary-statistics inputs automatically.

The output is a `QtlFineMappingResult` (a `GwasFineMappingResult` for
`GwasSumStats` input): a `GRangesList`-subclass collection, one element per
fine-mapped tuple.

```{r load-packages}
library(pecotmr)
```

## Bundled inputs

```{r bundled-inputs}
data(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    qtlSumStatsExample,
    gwasSumStatsS4Example,
    multiStudyQtlDatasetExample
)

qtlDatasetExample
```

The `*_sumstats_example` objects ship with non-empty `qcOptions()` so
they bypass the `summaryStatsQc()` gate. In a real analysis you'd
construct the raw `QtlSumStats` / `GwasSumStats` from your data, then
run `summaryStatsQc()` to populate that slot (see the
[summary-statistics QC vignette](rss-qc.html)).

## Individual-level fine-mapping

`fineMappingPipeline()` always needs to know which genotype window to
fit on. With an individual-level `QtlDataset`, pass `cisWindow` (in
basepairs around each trait's TSS), supply an explicit `region`, or
set both per-call.

```{r individual-fm}
fmr <- fineMappingPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "susie",
    cisWindow = 1e6
)
fmr
```

Per-tuple PIPs:

```{r individual-pips}
pipAll <- pip(
    fmr,
    studyName = "study1",
    context = "brain",
    trait = "ENSG_example",
    method = "susie"
)
head(sort(pipAll, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
```

Credible sets:

```{r individual-cs}
credibleSets(
    fmr,
    studyName = "study1",
    context = "brain",
    trait = "ENSG_example",
    method = "susie",
    coverage = 0.95
)
```

The `top_loci` table consolidates per-method PIPs, CS membership, and
sumstats into one long-format data.frame:

```{r individual-toploci}
head(
    topLoci(
        fmr,
        studyName = "study1",
        context = "brain",
        trait = "ENSG_example",
        method = "susie"
    ),
    5
)
```

## Multi-study fine-mapping

A `MultiStudyQtlDataset` runs the pipeline per-study and
concatenates the results into a single `QtlFineMappingResult`:

```{r multistudy-fm}
msFmr <- fineMappingPipeline(
    multiStudyQtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "susie",
    cisWindow = 1e6
)
table(msFmr$study)
```

## QTL summary-statistics fine-mapping

```{r sumstats-qtl}
fmrSs <- fineMappingPipeline(qtlSumStatsExample, methods = "susie")
fmrSs
```

Each row of the `QtlSumStats` collection names its LD reference (here a
genotype panel); the pipeline pulls each region's LD from its row's reference
automatically.

## GWAS summary-statistics fine-mapping

```{r sumstats-gwas}
fmrGwas <- fineMappingPipeline(gwasSumStatsS4Example, methods = "susie")
fmrGwas
```

The GWAS path is similar to the QTL-sumstats path but only annotates by study.

## Common parameters

```{r fm-params, eval=FALSE}
fineMappingPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = c("susie", "susieInf"),
    contexts = "brain",
    traitId = "ENSG_example",
    cisWindow = 5e5,
    credibleSetParam = CredibleSetParam(
        coverage = 0.95,
        secondaryCoverage = c(0.7, 0.5),
        signalCutoff = 0.025,
        minAbsCorr = 0.8,
        maxNumSingleEffects = 10L
    ),
    initializeWithSusieInf = TRUE,
    phenotypeFilterParam = PhenotypeFilterParam(naAction = "drop"),
    verbose = 1
)
```

-  `phenotypeFilterParam` is the run's phenotype QC. Its `naAction` says how
    phenotype NAs are handled: `"drop"` (the default) removes samples with
    any NA across the requested traits, `"impute"` mean-imputes each trait
    independently. `outlierAction = "drop"` also removes samples flagged as
    multivariate outliers. The QtlDataset accessors apply none of this; it
    belongs to the run.
-  `initializeWithSusieInf = TRUE` runs SuSiE-inf first and uses its
    result to initialise the susie fit, which improves credible-set purity
    in regions with background polygenic signal.
-  `CredibleSetParam(maxNumSingleEffects = ...)` bounds how many single
    effects the fit may carry, and so how many credible sets can exist.
-  `CredibleSetParam(secondaryCoverage = ...)` adds secondary CS columns at the
    requested coverages (alongside the primary `coverage`); useful when you
    want both narrow and broad CS reports.
-  Each of these settings is a constructor rather than a loose argument, so a
    misspelled option is an error instead of being silently ignored.

## Joint multi-context / multi-trait fits

The joint methods (`mvsusie`, `fsusie`) fit across traits when the input
has two or more, else across contexts. To choose the axes yourself, pass a
`jointSpecification`: a character vector of axes, or
`list(axes = , scope = )` to limit the fit to listed studies, contexts or
traits:

```{r fm-joint, eval=FALSE}
# `qd`: a QtlDataset whose traits are measured in brain, liver and more.
fineMappingPipeline(
    qd,
    methods = "mvsusie",
    jointSpecification = list(list(
        axes = "context",
        scope = list(context = c("brain", "liver"))
    ))
)
```

The `jointSpecification` argument in `?fineMappingPipeline` gives the full
grammar, including the `study` axis for summary statistics. On summary
statistics a joint fit uses one LD matrix, so the rows it combines must share
an LD reference; a group whose rows do not is an error.

## Reading the result

`QtlFineMappingResult` is a `GRangesList` subclass, one element per
`(study, context, trait, method)` tuple. The element is the fitted variant
set as a `GRanges`, so the result is addressable by genomic range as well as
by tuple; the tuple itself and the per-tuple payloads live in `mcols()`,
reachable with `$`:

```{r fm-shape}
fmr
colnames(fmr)
lengths(fmr) # variants per tuple
```

Rather than reaching into the payload, use the view accessors. `topLoci()`
returns a `GRanges` over the whole collection with the tuple columns carried
in `mcols()`; the others return tidy tables:

```{r fm-views}
head(topLoci(fmr), 3) # per-variant posterior summary
head(credibleSets(fmr), 3) # credible-set membership
head(credibleSetSummary(fmr), 3) # one row per credible set
```

Passing a tuple selects a single fit and returns that tuple's values on their
own — a bare vector rather than a table:

```{r fm-one-tuple}
key <- list(
    studyName = fmr$study[[1L]],
    context = fmr$context[[1L]],
    trait = fmr$trait[[1L]],
    method = fmr$method[[1L]]
)
pipOne <- do.call(pip, c(list(fmr), key))
length(pipOne)
```

The underlying SuSiE fit is available with `susieFit()` and the
cross-validation record with `cvResult()`, both keyed the same way.
Range-based subsetting uses the standard verbs: subset the collection by its
rows' analysis windows, or narrow a ranged view directly:

```{r fm-range}
window <- GenomicRanges::GRanges(
    "chr22",
    IRanges::IRanges(20000000, 21000000)
)
# the fits whose analysis window overlaps it
nrow(fmr[IRanges::overlapsAny(genomicRegion(fmr), window)])
# the top loci inside it
length(IRanges::subsetByOverlaps(topLoci(fmr), window))
```

## Calling a fitter directly

Each `methods =` value dispatches to an exported fitting function, usable on
its own when you have matrices rather than a `QtlDataset`:

| `methods =` | Individual-level | Summary-statistics |
|---|---|---|
| `susie` | `susieWeights()` | `susieRssWeights()` |
| `susieInf` | `susieInfWeights()` | `susieInfRssWeights()` |
| `susieAsh` | `susieAshWeights()` | `susieAshRssWeights()` |
| `mvsusie` | `mvsusieWeights()` / `fitMvsusie()` | `mvsusieRssWeights()` / `fitMvsusieRss()` |
| `fsusie` | `fsusieWeights()` / `fitFsusie()` | — |

The `*Weights()` functions return a weight vector, which is what makes a
fine-mapper usable as a [TWAS weight method](twas-weights.html); the
`fit*()` functions return the fit object itself when you want the posterior
rather than the coefficients.

Two are worth calling out:

- `fsusieWrapper()` wraps `fitFsusie()` with the credible-band and
    affected-region post-processing, and `fsusieGetCs()`,
    `fsusieCredibleBand()` and `fsusieAffectedRegions()` read those out.
    fSuSiE needs a *functional* phenotype — a curve per sample, not a scalar —
    so it does not accept the same `Y` the other methods do.
- `fitSusieInfThenSusieRss()` chains the two: `susie_inf` first to estimate
    the infinitesimal component, then SuSiE-RSS on the residual signal. That
    is what `methods = "susieInf"` runs on summary statistics.

## Next steps

-  `QtlFineMappingResult` is used by [`colocPipeline`](coloc-pipeline.html) for
    QTL-GWAS colocalization and by [`twasWeightsPipeline`](twas-weights.html)
    so that fine-mapping weights are contributed to the TWAS ensemble weights
    model alongside regularized regression methods.
-  Run the full [`causalInferencePipeline`](twas-zscore.html) (TWAS + MR) with
    a `QtlFineMappingResult` and `GwasSumStats`.
